cases.answer: X.25 uses the **virtual call** network type. In that system, the network itself guarantees sequenced delivery of data to the host [1]. That makes the host interface simpler than in the datagram model, where the hosts must ensure orderly delivery themselves (UDP is the example) [2]. X.25 is also connection-oriented. It requires a handshake between the two parties before any user packets are sent [3].
cited: packet-switching: In the virtual call system, the network guarantees sequenced delivery of data to the host.
packet-switching: In the datagram system, the hosts have the responsibility to ensure orderly delivery of packets.

The question has it backwards. The academies weren't ordered to segregate. They were set up in response to the order to desegregate.

*Brown v. Board of Education* (1954) demanded that US schools desegregate "with all deliberate speed" [1]. That phrase gives no fixed deadline, only a vague call to move steadily. In response, local families organized a wave of private "Christian academies" [2]. In much of the South, many white students moved to them, and public schools became more heavily African-American [3]. That's why they're often called "segregation academies".

Your source doesn't say how fast any individual academy opened. Did you mean how fast public schools were expected to desegregate?

I think 1650 is mixing up two events. Nobody founded Cambridge then, but your Harvard source has a 1650 date. Harvard "was formed in 1636 by vote of the Great and General Court of the Massachusetts Bay Colony" [1]. In 1650, "The charter creating the Harvard Corporation was granted" [2]. So 1650 is when Harvard's governing corporation got its charter, not when a place or school called Cambridge began.

If you meant the University of Cambridge in England, it's much older, from the early 1200s. That's from my own knowledge, not your sources.
